[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is one of several buildings that make up Amazon Web Services newly established data center campus in Madison County, Mississippi, spanning two industrial parks. The Mississippi Development Authority announced the initial investment on January 25, 2024, describing a 10 billion dollar commitment from AWS, which Governor Tate Reeves called the single largest capital investment in Mississippi history at the time, expected to create at least 1,000 high paying technology jobs and supported by Mississippi Major Economic Impact Authority funds for infrastructure, workforce training, and site preparation. Mississippi Public Broadcasting and other state and local outlets subsequently reported additional phases of investment, with cited figures growing over time, including references to 11 billion, 12 billion, and eventually a cumulative 25 billion dollar figure across the company broader Mississippi footprint in later coverage. Because these later, larger figures were reported across a sequence of separate announcements rather than confirmed together in a single AWS owned publication found during this research, they are presented here as a record of escalating public commitments rather than as one fixed, current total. This is one of AWS newest major campuses among its US facilities, still in a rapid buildout phase as of this research. AWS does not publish individual building addresses, capacities, or specifications, so this specific building construction date, square footage, and critical IT megawattage cannot be independently confirmed beyond its general location within the Madison County campus.

profile.disclosure_policy: Confirmed directly on AWS own Global Infrastructure page (aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/): AWS does not publish specific street addresses or per-building technical specifications (square footage, power capacity in MW) for its data centers, as a matter of stated security and operational policy. AWS states each Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, each with independent power, cooling, and physical security, but does not break this down to individual facility addresses. This session confirmed this disclosure policy directly rather than assuming it, and applies this finding to AWS records that otherwise have no facility specific address, square footage, planned capacity, or critical_it_mw on file. This is a company wide policy finding, not a statement that no such facility exists at this location.

reading.body:
This facility is one of several buildings within Amazon Web Services' newly established data center campus in Madison County, Mississippi, announced in January 2024 as a $10 billion investment and described by Mississippi's governor as the largest capital investment in the state's history at that time. AWS does not publish per-building power capacity, square footage, or technical specifications as a stated company policy, so the critical IT megawattage and rack density of this specific building cannot be independently confirmed. The campus spans two industrial parks and is in active buildout phase, with AWS having announced subsequent phases at figures reported to exceed $25 billion cumulatively across its Mississippi footprint, though these larger figures come from state and local outlets reporting a sequence of announcements rather than a single AWS-owned source.

Mississippi has four mapped data center facilities on record and zero published megawatt figures from operator specification pages, making this the highest-ranked facility in the state by the absence of any disclosed capacity. The state context reflects Mississippi's nascent position in the data center landscape: no operator has published power specifications for any facility in the state, and mapped facilities are drawn from OpenStreetMap rather than facility operator disclosures.

For a reader assessing whether this campus matters to AI scaling, the limiting factor is opacity. The investment scale and job creation numbers are substantial and verified from state sources. The compute capacity, power draw, and grid integration—the metrics that determine whether this campus contributes to solving AI's binding constraint—remain unpublished by AWS and cannot be derived from available data.
